cards.title: Match Product Development to a Specific Business Problem
cards.summary: Develop new products to solve one of three problems — margin, volume, or cash flow — rather than because an idea seems cool.
cards.use_when: Scoping a new product or category and deciding which business problem it must solve.

cards.title: Price SKUs Differently Instead of One Flat Price
cards.summary: Demand differs across colorways and sizes, so price-map each SKU to actual demand — and price outliers down to liquidate them.
cards.use_when: Setting or adjusting SKU-level prices, managing slow-moving colorways/sizes, and keeping the ad account healthy.

cards.title: Test New Product Demand Before Placing a Large PO
cards.summary: Run small batch orders, pre-orders, or in-house fast manufacturing to validate demand and de-risk the biggest killer — bad inventory buys.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to test demand for a new SKU or category before committing to a full production order.

cards.title: Build a Demand Plan to Support the Inventory Plan
cards.summary: Before placing a PO, map exactly how each unit will be sold — email/SMS, influencers, and paid media at a defined efficiency — so volume isn't divorced from demand creation.
cards.use_when: Planning a new product launch, category expansion, or any PO where you're committing inventory dollars.

cards.title: Invest in Story-Making, Not Just Ad Iteration
cards.summary: Iterating on hooks and creative optimizes for a local maximum; large returns come from novel stories that unlock new cohorts and distribution.
cards.use_when: Designing a creative strategy and allocating time between iteration testing and building new concepts/campaigns.

cards.title: Avoid Overspending Past the Marginal Frontier
cards.summary: Inefficient ad dollars beyond the point where the next dollar loses money are the clearest cash-flow killer.
cards.use_when: Reviewing media spend for waste and deciding where to cut spend to protect cash.

cards.title: Align Labor Cost with Seasonal Revenue (12% of Lowest Month)
cards.summary: Set baseline full-time payroll at roughly 12% of your lowest revenue month and flex-staff everything above that instead of carrying flat FTE cost through valleys.
cards.use_when: Planning headcount and staffing costs for an ecommerce business with strong seasonality.

cards.title: Acquire New Customers Before Peak Realization Moments
cards.summary: Build large-scale new-customer acquisition moments ahead of Black Friday and other peaks so the existing base over-delivers during the value-realization window.
cards.use_when: Planning the Q4 marketing calendar and sequencing acquisition versus retention campaigns.

cards.title: Consolidate the Marketing Team into a 'Profit Engineer' Role
cards.summary: The source argues media buying, creative strategy, retention, and forecasting for one brand are no longer four full-time jobs but one combined accountable role.
cards.use_when: Designing marketing team structure and deciding which roles to keep in-house versus consolidate or automate.

cards.title: Test Whether AI-Only Creative Beats Human-in-the-Loop
cards.summary: A cited study found AI working independently outperformed humans-alone and humans-briefing-AI workflows; the source argues human preconceptions can cap creative performance.
cards.use_when: Designing the creative production workflow and deciding how much human judgment to apply versus letting AI run independently.

cards.title: Adapt the MVP and Constraint Logic to Inventory and Media Decisions
cards.summary: Constraint, MVP, and demand-planning frameworks from a turnaround operator apply directly to inventory buys, media allocation, and category bets.
cards.use_when: Applying strategy frameworks from broader business or turnaround contexts to concrete ecommerce inventory, pricing, and category-expansion decisions.

cards.title: Run three AI creative workflows as a test
cards.summary: Test human-only, human-briefed-AI, and AI-independent creative workflows to see which produces the best-performing ad variants for your store.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much human input to put into ad creative generation for paid acquisition.

cards.title: Measure AI revenue contribution including LLM commerce
cards.summary: Track whether LLMs become a real revenue driver, defined by the source as up to 10% of revenue sourced from or occurring within LLMs for some businesses.
cards.use_when: Forecasting marketing mix, budgeting for AI-commerce readiness, or deciding whether to invest in LLM product-feed setup for your store.

cards.title: Follow transaction toward discovery
cards.summary: Put your transactions where people already discover products, because transaction always moves to the point of discovery.
cards.use_when: Deciding which sales channels to open or prioritize (TikTok Shop, Amazon, LLM, retail).

cards.title: Fit creative format to product complexity and funnel stage
cards.summary: Match ad format to how much information a buyer needs, then place the explanation either in the ad or the landing page.
cards.use_when: Choosing between static image and video ads and deciding what the landing page must do for a specific product.

cards.title: Test distinctive ecommerce creative while controlling unprofitable ad spend
cards.summary: Use the source's preference for fresh creative as a testing hypothesis within contribution and inventory limits.
cards.use_when: Managing a live ad account and planning creative rotation for the next quarter.

cards.title: Treat creative as a sales obligation, not art
cards.summary: Judge creative by whether it drives a business outcome, using David Ogilvy's principle that it is only creative if it sells.
cards.use_when: Evaluating creative concepts or briefing a creative team or agency for your store.

cards.title: Write good-role / bad-role documents
cards.summary: Define what a role looks like when done badly as well as well, using the good/bad software engineer format.
cards.use_when: Writing job descriptions or onboarding docs for ecommerce roles like media buyer, retention manager, or merchandiser.

cards.title: Map influencer types to what you actually need
cards.summary: Influencers deliver trust, distribution, or content assets, and your job is to know which you need.
cards.use_when: Planning influencer or creator spend for your store and choosing who to work with.

cards.title: Build a media arm to drive negative CAC
cards.summary: Use owned media to offset marketing cost so acquisition can become profit-generating rather than a pure expense.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in content, podcast, or media as a customer acquisition channel for your brand.

cards.title: Align dashboards to financial incentives
cards.summary: If financial incentives don't match the dashboard you show people, their behavior won't match it either.
cards.use_when: Setting team metrics or performance incentives for ecommerce roles like media buying, merchandising, or retention.

cards.title: Expect harder output-expectation setting from AI
cards.summary: AI raises the ceiling on possible output so fast that rightsizing team expectations becomes the hardest management problem.
cards.use_when: Setting creative volume targets or performance expectations for a marketing or ecommerce team now that AI tools are in use.

cards.title: Start with free cash flow, not net income, to judge business health
cards.summary: Use operating cash flow and capital spending alongside net income to assess an ecommerce store's available cash.
cards.use_when: Monthly or quarterly financial review of an ecommerce store, when net income looks healthy but the cash balance is shrinking or we are unsure whether to hire, buy inventory or take on debt.

cards.title: Map the three cash flow statement sections to store activities
cards.summary: Operating, investing and financing sections each capture different cash movements, and knowing which section an ecommerce transaction belongs to prevents misreading cash health.
cards.use_when: When setting up or reviewing an ecommerce cash flow statement and deciding where to record inventory buys, software build costs, loan drawdowns or owner distributions.

cards.title: Why inventory purchases make a profitable store run out of cash
cards.summary: Buying stock in large lumps hits cash in the purchase month while the cost only reaches the P&L when goods sell, so profitable periods can coincide with cash shortages.
cards.use_when: Planning inventory replenishment or a seasonal stock buy for an ecommerce store, or explaining why a high-revenue month did not improve the bank balance.

cards.title: Discount-driven revenue spikes lower gross margin percentage
cards.summary: In the case study, the month where orders more than doubled during a sale also saw gross margin percentage drop, so monitor margin percentage alongside revenue volume.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a sitewide sale, promotion or discount event, and evaluating the margin consequence after the event.

cards.title: Capitalised software development hides cash outflow from the P&L
cards.summary: Capitalising developer payroll pushes cost to the balance sheet and spreads it over its useful life, so the P&L shows a fraction of the actual cash being spent.
cards.use_when: Budgeting for building or extending a custom storefront, app or platform with an in-house or contracted engineering team, and reviewing why cash is leaving faster than reported expenses suggest.

cards.title: Schedule cash tax payments using the store's actual tax calendar
cards.summary: Profit-based monthly tax estimates can differ from actual payment dates; reserve cash for the confirmed schedule.
cards.use_when: Forecasting store cash needs around quarter-end and reconciling monthly reported profit with actual cash movement in the bank.

cards.title: Debt principal repayments never appear on the income statement
cards.summary: Only interest on debt hits the P&L; principal repayments show up on the balance sheet and financing section, so loan drawdowns and repayments distort cash without changing reported profit.
cards.use_when: Managing a store line of credit, merchant cash advance or term loan, and judging whether reported profitability reflects the real cash burden of debt.

cards.title: Reconcile a profitable month against a negative free cash flow month
cards.summary: Working through the case study month by month shows how to attribute a cash shortfall to specific balance sheet movements rather than to profitability.
cards.use_when: After a month where the store reported a profit but the bank balance dropped, to identify the exact causes before deciding on corrective action.

cards.title: Separate near-cash expenses from non-cash items when reading the P&L
cards.summary: Most operating expense lines equal their cash outlay, but depreciation and product cost do not, so identify which expenses reflect money actually leaving the bank.
cards.use_when: Reviewing the store's operating expense structure to decide where cash can realistically be cut versus where cuts only change reported profit.

cards.title: Track the three statements together to see what the P&L omits
cards.summary: The income statement captures unit economics, the balance sheet reveals asset, debt and inventory movements, and the cash flow statement ties them into actual cash change.
cards.use_when: Building or reviewing the store's monthly reporting pack, or when a single statement gives a misleading picture of ecommerce health.

cards.title: COGS Drives Unit Economics and Valuation
cards.summary: Why COGS accuracy matters for ecommerce operators: it sets the cash left per unit for marketing and R&D and drives gross margin used in valuations.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product can fund its own acquisition and reinvestment, or preparing gross margin figures for investors or lenders.

cards.title: Separate inbound inventory freight from customer delivery costs
cards.summary: Document the cost's economic purpose and accounting policy, then include variable selling and delivery costs in ecommerce contribution analysis.
cards.use_when: Setting up the chart of accounts or reviewing shipping cost treatment for an ecommerce store that ships physical products to customers.

cards.title: CPG vs SaaS Cost Structures and Margin Benchmarks
cards.summary: CPG/manufacturing carries high tangible COGS and 20-40% gross margins; SaaS carries lower labor/server COGS and 70-90% gross margins.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product model to build or expand, or sanity-checking whether your store's gross margin is in a normal range for its category.

cards.title: Balance Sheet to P&L Timing for Inventory Versus Services
cards.summary: CPG costs sit on the balance sheet as inventory until sale, while many SaaS costs like wages hit the P&L immediately.
cards.use_when: Forecasting cash and monthly profitability, or explaining to a founder-investor why a stock build-up hurts cash before it hits COGS.

cards.title: Classify ecommerce customer support costs consistently
cards.summary: Document the cost's economic purpose and accounting policy, then include variable selling and delivery costs in ecommerce contribution analysis.
cards.use_when: Allocating team costs for a subscription or membership store so that gross margin and retention investment are reported correctly.

cards.title: Separate partner commissions from product acquisition cost
cards.summary: Document the cost's economic purpose and accounting policy, then include variable selling and delivery costs in ecommerce contribution analysis.
cards.use_when: Recording affiliate, marketplace or channel-partner commissions for an ecommerce store to keep gross margin meaningful.

cards.title: Tie Server and Hosting Costs to Business Usage
cards.summary: Cloud costs (AWS/Azure) left unchecked rise quickly; reconcile them to customer or usage growth with engineering.
cards.use_when: Running a hosted or usage-based digital store, app or subscription platform where cloud spend is a major COGS line.

cards.title: Waste Control: Expiry Rotation, Fire Sales and Inventory Controls
cards.summary: Reduce COGS leakage by moving near-expiry stock first, using fire sales to clear aged goods, logging stock in/out, and counting periodically.
cards.use_when: Managing perishable or seasonal inventory and shrink in an ecommerce warehouse or 3PL.

cards.title: Correct COGS Gives a Trustworthy Gross Margin Signal
cards.summary: Accurate elements and timing of COGS produce the gross margin that informs unit economics and business decisions.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly accounts before making product-line, pricing or discontinue decisions.

cards.title: Run the 3x3 loop: Commit, Check-in, Close for ecommerce teams
cards.summary: High-performing teams agree on goals, roles and norms upfront, then repeatedly check in and close the gap between what they say and what they do.
cards.use_when: Standing up or fixing the team structure behind a store's merchandising, content, ads or fulfillment operations.

cards.title: Write goals you can actually check against
cards.summary: Explicit, conversational agreement on goals, roles and norms beats silent assumptions and lets teams detect drift later.
cards.use_when: Setting quarterly goals for a store team or agreeing who owns which channel before a busy trading period.

cards.title: Close the saying-doing gap with small, environment-aware steps
cards.summary: The core of team improvement is shrinking the gap between stated intentions and daily behavior using small targeted changes and realistic optimism.
cards.use_when: When a store team keeps agreeing on plans in meetings but day-to-day execution on pricing, listings or fulfilment keeps slipping.

cards.title: Three guidelines for better check-in conversations
cards.summary: Pay attention to styles, hold one-on-ones, and focus on a few topics to make team check-ins productive rather than performative.
cards.use_when: Running team rituals such as weekly ops standups, launch retros or trading reviews where conversations get stuck or unproductive.

cards.title: Match the work to teams vs. individuals
cards.summary: Not every task belongs to a team: expert, highly creative and time-critical work is often faster and better done by one person, while multi-perspective problems suit teams.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to assign a store task — e.g. writing a product page, setting pricing, or solving a merchandising problem — to an individual or a group.

cards.title: Common team failure modes: hero reliance, plan-worship, role neglect
cards.summary: Three recurring mistakes undermine teams: over-relying on one person, focusing on the plan instead of execution, and never defining who does what.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why a store launch or seasonal plan stalls after a good planning meeting.

cards.title: Build psychological safety so people actually speak up
cards.summary: Psychological safety — people feeling able to share thoughts — improves decisions and collaboration, but most people withhold what they think.
cards.use_when: When store meetings produce silence or polite agreement but the real problems (stockouts, bad creative, weak margins) surface only later.

cards.title: Know when to go fast and when to go slow
cards.summary: Match speed to task type: skip heavy team process when speed is essential, and slow down for formation and multi-perspective decisions.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much process to apply to a same-day flash sale versus a long-term category or assortment decision.

cards.title: Build landed unit cost and contribution per ecommerce order
cards.summary: Calculate product and delivery costs separately from advertising and overhead so pricing decisions use a consistent contribution measure.
cards.use_when: Pricing a product, deciding whether a SKU is viable, or setting up daily profit reporting in Shopify/Triple Whale.

cards.title: Write a tech pack to control supplier quality and prove non-conformance
cards.summary: A tech pack documents drawings, fabric GSM, measurements, hardware, graphics and labels so manufacturing errors can be proven and disputed.
cards.use_when: Developing or re-sourcing any physical product, especially apparel, before placing a large purchase order.

cards.title: Negotiate MOQ, price and lead time as one trade-off set
cards.summary: Treat supplier MOQ, unit price and manufacturing lead time as the three levers to balance against cash flow and retail price.
cards.use_when: Selecting a supplier or placing a first or repeat purchase order.

cards.title: Order against the outputs: operations as an input→process→output system
cards.summary: Model operations as inputs → processes → outputs, and judge every change by whether it improves the customer-facing output while cutting inputs and process load.
cards.use_when: Deciding which operational initiative to fund or fix (warehouse change, automation, forecasting hire) and how to justify it against marketing spend.

cards.title: Build a critical path to hit launch and seasonal deadlines
cards.summary: A critical path sequences every product-development step with durations and dates so slips are visible and you avoid missing peak trading windows.
cards.use_when: Planning any product launch or seasonal buying cycle where missing a ship date means stranded inventory (e.g. Christmas).

cards.title: Forecast demand on an in-stock window, not a raw calendar period
cards.summary: Base forecasts on periods you were actually in stock and on comparable prior-year/month velocity, then apply a growth rate.
cards.use_when: Replenishment planning for any SKU before placing a purchase order.

cards.title: Set lead time, days-of-stock and safety stock inputs in the forecast tool
cards.summary: Feed supplier lead time, target days of stock and a small safety-stock buffer into the planner so sell-out and reorder-point outputs are realistic.
cards.use_when: Configuring replenishment thresholds and deciding how much working capital to commit to inventory.

cards.title: Use purchase orders as the single cross-functional source of truth
cards.summary: A PO is more than an invoice — it must be visible to finance, ops, marketing and customer service so stock arrival and discontinuations are coordinated.
cards.use_when: Raising, landing or discontinuing any stock order, and coordinating teams around inbound inventory.

cards.title: Protect against 3PL failure with SLAs and multi-warehouse RFPs
cards.summary: Specify picked-on-time, delivered-on-time and cycle-count SLAs, and run a request-for-pricing across multiple warehouses to create competitive bids.
cards.use_when: Selecting or reviewing a 3PL, or negotiating fulfilment rates and service guarantees.

cards.title: Keep import duties and collected sales taxes separate in the cost model
cards.summary: Use verified import-cost inputs and net-revenue reporting rather than treating all tax amounts as the same expense.
cards.use_when: Building landed cost for cross-border sourcing or setting up tax handling in the store backend.

cards.title: Choose supplier co-development vs independent product design
cards.summary: Compare supplier co-development with independently commissioned design on cost, control and documented rights.
cards.use_when: Committing to a product development route for a new or differentiated product.

cards.title: Run forecasting continuously to avoid the two existential inventory failures
cards.summary: Selling out or over-ordering are both business-ending risks; forecast so cash isn't trapped in inventory while peak is covered.
cards.use_when: Deciding SKU expansion and seasonal buy quantities under cash constraints.

cards.title: Purchase order visibility across departments
cards.summary: A PO is a cross-functional document; keep it in a shared internal system so finance, ops, marketing and customer service act on the same truth.
cards.use_when: Setting up or auditing how purchase orders are recorded and shared before a replenishment order is placed or while stock is in transit.

cards.title: Auditing 3PL invoices against actual order volume
cards.summary: Reconstruct per-order 3PL costs from your own sales data monthly rather than accepting the invoice at face value.
cards.use_when: Monthly reconciliation of a 3PL bill, or comparing 3PL quotes when switching providers.

cards.title: Running an RFP to select a 3PL
cards.summary: Use a structured request-for-pricing with forecasts and product dimensions to make 3PLs compete, then inspect facilities before signing.
cards.use_when: Choosing or replacing a third-party logistics provider.

cards.title: Writing an SLA with pick-time penalties for peak periods
cards.summary: Make pick and ship commitments explicit and attach consequences so peak-season failures do not become your brand's negative reviews.
cards.use_when: Negotiating or renewing a 3PL contract, especially before Black Friday or Christmas.

cards.title: Designing the customer service tier split
cards.summary: Route simple tickets to international agents and nuanced tickets to local agents close to internal teams — and be sceptical of the assumption that offshore is always cheaper.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to staff and structure the customer support function, particularly when scaling past a few agents.

cards.title: Cost per ticket and resolution-time diagnostics
cards.summary: Track cost per service, resolution time and touch points to find whether support problems come from systems, information access, or staffing.
cards.use_when: Reviewing customer service performance and support cost during monthly operations or before peak planning.

cards.title: Forecast-driven support capacity planning
cards.summary: Use the sales forecast to onboard and train support agents ahead of peak rather than reactively hiring when ticket volume spikes.
cards.use_when: Quarterly support headcount planning, or deciding when to add agents before a promotional period.

cards.title: Deciding when to buy an ERP
cards.summary: Use revenue scale, not discomfort, as the trigger for moving from spreadsheets and accounting software to an ERP.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to invest in an ERP or keep running POs, freight and inventory on accounting software plus shared sheets.

cards.title: Why manual operations sheets fail
cards.summary: Shared operational sheets only work with disciplined, scheduled updating; stale data causes other teams to act on false assumptions.
cards.use_when: Assigning ownership and update cadence for PO, freight or inventory trackers used by multiple teams.

cards.title: Choosing a freight provider on competing quotes
cards.summary: Use two to three local freight providers competing on monthly rates, and push their shipment data into your internal tracker.
cards.use_when: Arranging container or air freight from a supplier to your 3PL or warehouse.

cards.title: Distinguish teams from groups before assigning work
cards.summary: Use the group-versus-team distinction to decide whether a work unit needs shared accountability or just coordinated reporting.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to structure recurring store operations (e.g., fulfillment crew, content team) versus a one-off launch squad.

cards.title: Judge team effectiveness by output vs sum of individual output
cards.summary: Use the synergy test — team output should exceed the sum of individual outputs — as the operating definition of an effective team.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether a cross-functional squad (merchandising + content + paid media) is worth its coordination overhead.

cards.title: Diagnose poor team performance across internal and external causes
cards.summary: Check external system factors (design, culture, selection, training, rewards) alongside internal process before blaming the people.
cards.use_when: When a store team repeatedly misses deadlines (restock plans, campaign launches, content calendar) and the instinct is to replace individuals.

cards.title: Set team size and skill mix deliberately
cards.summary: Treat team size and composition as design variables that cause failure when wrong, rather than defaults.
cards.use_when: Composing a launch squad, creative pod, or fulfillment shift before work begins.

cards.title: Run Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, Adjourning as a planning lens
cards.summary: Anticipate each development stage's characteristic behavior so you intervene with the right action instead of fighting normal friction.
cards.use_when: Onboarding a new store team, integrating an acquisition, or reading conflict in an existing squad as a stage rather than a crisis.

cards.title: Convert vision into a mission and shared goals the team owns
cards.summary: Build team direction top-down from organizational vision to team mission to jointly set goals so members know what is expected and commit.
cards.use_when: Writing the charter for a new squad — for example a retention team, content studio, or marketplace expansion pod.

cards.title: Work through the five-step commitment ladder before asking buy-in
cards.summary: Treat resistance to a new initiative as an unresolved pre-commitment process and address it before demanding accountability.
cards.use_when: Rolling out a new process (new WMS, new ad platform, new PDP workflow) where the team nods but does not adopt.

cards.title: Diagnose commitment blockers by listing unknowns
cards.summary: Surface and research the unknowns behind hesitation rather than reading hesitation as disloyalty.
cards.use_when: When a key operator stalls on adopting a new process, taking on a new channel, or committing to a stretch target.

cards.title: Clarify roles with the Role Analysis Technique
cards.summary: Define a focal role jointly with the team and record it as a written role profile to kill mutual 'not doing their job' assumptions.
cards.use_when: After a reorg, a new hire, or when two functions collide (e.g., merchandising vs. paid media over who owns creative).
